overview.headline: A copper-binding tripeptide marketed for hair growth. The evidence is one 2007 laboratory study on hair follicles in a dish.
overview.lede: AHK-Cu is the tripeptide alanine-histidine-lysine bound to a copper ion, a cousin of the better-known cosmetic copper peptide GHK-Cu. The only published human-tissue evidence is a Korean study from 2007 in which it lengthened plucked human hair follicles kept alive in culture and made dermal papilla cells multiply. No clinical trial on people has been published or registered. Nothing is approved, and the vials sold as AHK-Cu for injection or home-made serums are unregulated products.

mechanism.intro: Copper peptides are thought to deliver copper to enzymes in skin and hair and to nudge growth signals.

parts.name: Copper carrier
parts.text: The tripeptide binds a copper ion and may help deliver it to copper-dependent enzymes involved in collagen cross-linking and tissue repair. This is the rationale for all copper peptides in cosmetics.

parts.name: Dermal papilla
parts.text: The dermal papilla is the cluster of cells at the base of a hair follicle that drives growth. In the 2007 study AHK-Cu made these cells multiply and raised the Bcl-2/Bax ratio, a sign of reduced cell death.

parts.name: Fibroblasts
parts.text: Earlier work on skin fibroblasts, cited as background in the 2007 paper, reported more VEGF (a vessel-growth factor) and less TGF-beta1 with the tripeptide-copper complex.

more.title: More: AHK-Cu and GHK-Cu are not the same
paras: GHK-Cu (glycine-histidine-lysine-copper) is a natural fragment found in human blood, with decades of cosmetic use and a few small human skin studies. AHK-Cu swaps the first amino acid and has no comparable record. Marketing routinely blurs the two. Sources are listed under the Status tab.

results.headline: No human results. One experiment on cultured hair follicles.
results.lede: There is no trial of AHK-Cu in people, with or without placebo, so there is no chart.

items.t: Human hair follicles kept alive in culture grew longer when AHK-Cu was added at very low concentrations (10^-12 to 10^-9 M).

Cultured human dermal papilla cells multiplied faster; markers of programmed cell death (cleaved caspase-3 and PARP) fell and the Bcl-2/Bax ratio rose. The drop in the number of dying cells at the highest concentration was not statistically significant.
No published hair-growth study in animals was found.
None. No clinical trial of AHK-Cu, topical or injected, has been published or registered.

more.title: More: why a dish result is a long way from a scalp
paras: Cultured follicles respond to many substances that do nothing on a living head, because the culture removes blood supply, hormones, immune cells and the skin barrier. The approved hair-loss drugs earned their place through randomised trials with hair counts; AHK-Cu has not been through that step.

effects.headline: Unknown. Never given to people in a study.
effects.lede: There is no human safety data for AHK-Cu by any route. What follows is what is known about copper peptides generally and about the risks of untested injectables.

disc.title: Stopping because of side effects
disc.text: Not applicable. No human study has given AHK-Cu.

unique.title: Copper, and the FDA's view of injected copper peptides
unique.text: On skin, copper peptides are widely used in cosmetics and reports are mainly of mild irritation; copper itself is toxic in excess. Injected AHK-Cu has never been studied. Reviewing the related GHK-Cu for injectable routes, the FDA cited a risk of immune reactions from peptide aggregation and impurities and limited human data (list current April 2026). Those concerns apply at least as strongly to AHK-Cu, which has less data still.

more.title: More: what a trial would monitor for
paras: A topical study would track scalp irritation and hair counts; an injection study would add immune reactions, copper levels and liver function. None of this has been done.

more.title: More: the good side effects
paras: None reported in humans. Longer follicles in culture are the hypothesis a trial would test.

urgent.title: Symptoms doctors treat as urgent after any injected product
items: Swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing, hives
Fever, spreading redness or pus at an injection site
Persistent nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain (possible copper excess)
Dark urine, yellowing of the skin or eyes
urgent.note: Anyone with these symptoms should get medical care right away and bring the product with them.

levels.nopk: No human pharmacokinetic data exist for AHK-Cu by any route. The only concentrations ever studied are those added to culture dishes, which say nothing about what reaches a follicle from a serum or an injection.

stats.lbl: amino acids plus one copper ion
the only setting in which AHK-Cu's effects have been measured

explain.t: The simulator needs a human half-life and a tested dose range. Neither exists.

explain.b: Why 'worked at tiny concentrations' is not a dose.
explain.t: The 2007 effects appeared at trillionths to billionths of a mole per litre in culture fluid. No one knows what concentration a scalp serum or an injection produces at the follicle, or whether more is better or worse.

more.title: More: what this page cannot tell you
paras: It cannot tell you whether a product sold as AHK-Cu contains the peptide, carries copper, penetrates the scalp, or grows hair. No human study has addressed any of these.

trials.headline: No human trials have been run.
trials.lede: AHK-Cu has never been tested on people in a registered study, as a serum or an injection.

more.title: More: how hair-growth treatments are normally proven
paras: Approved treatments were tested in randomised, placebo-controlled trials lasting six months to a year, counting hairs in a marked patch of scalp. Nothing of the kind exists for AHK-Cu.

running.title: No human trials
items: None registered or published as of October 2026.
The sole peer-reviewed study (2007) used follicles and cells in culture.

find.text: If a trial is ever registered it will appear on the public registry. Searching today returns nothing.

status.headline: Not approved anywhere. Never reviewed by any regulator for human use.

items.label: Canada: not authorized
items.text: Health Canada has not authorized any AHK-Cu product. It treats injectable peptides as prescription drugs, said in April 2026 that unauthorized injectable peptide drugs are illegal in Canada, and in July 2026 obtained a permanent injunction against the Quebec seller Canlab Research.

items.label: US: not approved
items.text: The FDA has never approved AHK-Cu, and it does not appear on the FDA's Category 2 or withdrawn-nomination lists for compounding (April 2026). Its relative GHK-Cu (injectable routes) left Category 2 in April 2026 and is due for advisory committee review by February 2027. Sold for people, AHK-Cu is an unapproved drug; the FDA's August 24, 2026 warning letters rejected 'research use only' disclaimers.

items.label: Sport: prohibited
items.text: AHK-Cu is not named on the 2026 WADA Prohibited List, but with no approval anywhere for human use it falls under the S0 clause, prohibited at all times.

cards.title: What 'research use only' means
cards.text: Vials sold as AHK-Cu carry 'for research use only' labels. That describes a product meant for laboratory work, not people. It does not mean the contents were tested, and it does not make the sale legal once the seller markets the product for human use.
items: Health Canada: injectable peptides are prescription drugs; unauthorized ones are illegal to sell (2025 and 2026 notices).
FDA warning letters, August 24, 2026: the disclaimer does not control when a website shows the product is intended as a drug for people.

cards.title: Symptoms to take to a doctor
cards.text: Anyone who has injected a product sold as AHK-Cu, or applied one to broken skin, should tell a doctor, especially with any of the following:
items: Fever, redness or pus at an injection site
Persistent nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain
Dark urine or yellow skin or eyes
cards.note: Report a reaction to MedEffect Canada (canada.ca/medeffect) or, in the U.S., FDA MedWatch (fda.gov/medwatch).

more.title: More: the copper-peptide market
paras: Copper peptides are a legitimate cosmetic category in finished products that have passed a safety assessment. The 'research peptide' version sits outside that system and borrows the category's reputation without its controls.
